extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, prose fiction writers, and storytellers (film/novel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing a story's Spine/Through-line and the Central Plot's Inciting Incident, plus how to build progressive complications, points-of-no-return, and meaningful conflict so the tale sustains dramatic momentum to its Obligatory Scene and Climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Spine of the story (Through-line / Super-objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The energy of a protagonist’s desire forms the critical element of design known as the Spine of the story (AKA Through-line or Super-objective). The Spine is the deep desire in and effort by the protagonist to restore the balance of life. It’s the primary unifying force that holds all other story elements together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene, image, and word should ultimately be an aspect of the Spine, relating causally or thematically to this core of desire and action. Examples: Bond’s Spine is a conscious objective ('to defeat the arch-villain'); other films (The Crying Game, Carnal Knowledge, Mrs. Soffel) show unconscious desires driving the Spine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious desire versus conscious objective as Spine
rubrics_metrics.description: If the protagonist has no unconscious desire, then his conscious objective becomes the Spine. If, on the other hand, the protagonist has an unconscious desire, this becomes the Spine of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unconscious desire is always more powerful and durable, permitting more complex characters who may repeatedly change their conscious desire. Example: Bond has no unconscious desire (conscious goal holds the film); Jonathan in CARNAL KNOWLEDGE demonstrates an unchanging unconscious desire beneath shifting conscious wants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the protagonist's Object of Desire (Quest form)
rubrics_metrics.description: All stories take the form of a Quest: an event throws a character's life out of balance, arousing conscious and/or unconscious desire for that which will restore balance, launching him on a quest for his Object of Desire against forces of antagonism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand a story's Quest form, identify the protagonist's Object of Desire by penetrating his psychology and answering 'What does he want?' The Object may be material (someone to love) or spiritual (inner growth). Examples: MOONSTRUCK, BIG, JAWS, TENDER MERCIES.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident: cause and necessity to be onscreen (Central Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Inciting Incident happens in only one of two ways: randomly or causally, either by coincidence or by decision. The Inciting Incident of the Central Plot must happen onscreen — not in the Backstory, not between scenes offscreen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each subplot has its own Inciting Incident which may or may not be onscreen, but the presence of the audience at the Central Plot’s Inciting Incident is crucial because it provokes the Major Dramatic Question and projects the Obligatory Scene into the audience's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident must provoke the Major Dramatic Question and project the Obligatory Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: When the audience experiences an Inciting Incident, the film’s Major Dramatic Question is provoked to mind. Witnessing the Inciting Incident projects an image of the Obligatory Scene (AKA Crisis) into the audience’s imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Obligatory Scene is an event the audience knows it must see before the story can end; having teased the audience into anticipating this moment, the writer is obligated to show it. Examples: JAWS projects an image of shark vs sheriff; LA NOTTE, JALSAGHER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement guideline: locate Inciting Incident within first 25% (rule of thumb)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule of thumb, the first major event of the Central Plot occurs within the first 25 percent of the telling. For a two-hour feature film, locate the Central Plot’s Inciting Incident somewhere within the first half-hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It could be the very first thing or later (examples: SULLIVAN'S TRAVELS, ON THE WATERFRONT, TAXI DRIVER, ROCKY, CASABLANCA). If it arrives much later than ~15 minutes, boredom becomes a risk; however bring it in 'as soon as possible...but not until the moment is ripe.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident must hook the audience emotionally and rationally
rubrics_metrics.description: An Inciting Incident must 'hook' the audience, producing a deep and complete response that is both emotional and rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The event must pull at feelings and cause the audience to ask the Major Dramatic Question and imagine the Obligatory Scene; decide how much the audience needs to know about protagonist/world to have a full response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality/germane-ness of the Inciting Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the Inciting Incident must be germane to the world, characters, and genre surrounding it. In the right context just a gesture or look can function as an Inciting Incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Does it radically upset the balance of the protagonist’s life? Does it arouse desire to restore balance? Does it inspire the conscious desire for a specific object? Does it bring to life unconscious desire? Examples: ORDINARY PEOPLE's Inciting Incident is a mother scraping French toast into a garbage disposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing/creating the Inciting Incident (what-if extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: To create the Inciting Incident ask: What is the worst possible thing that could happen to my protagonist? How could that turn out to be the best possible thing? Or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals and extremes to reach limits of life. Examples used as prompts: KRAMER VS KRAMER, AN UNMARRIED WOMAN, DEATH IN VENICE, THE GODFATHER PART II. The Inciting Incident should jolt the protagonist's life from its pattern so chaos invades the character’s universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection and foreshadowing of the Obligatory Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident should project an image of the Obligatory Scene into the audience's imagination; linking the Inciting Incident to the Crisis is an aspect of Foreshadowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every choice—genre, setting, character, mood, each line of dialogue or image—foreshadows. The primary component of foreshadowing is projection of the Obligatory Scene by the Inciting Incident; mishandling this causes audience dissatisfaction even if they can't name the missing element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive Complications (Act Two body of story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive Complications form the body of the story from Inciting Incident to Crisis/Climax: to complicate is to make life difficult; to complicate progressively is to generate more and more conflict, creating a succession of events that pass points of no return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressions build by drawing upon greater capacities from characters, demanding greater willpower and increasing risk, constantly passing points of no return in magnitude/quality of action. Do not allow the story to retreat to lesser actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Points of No Return (eliminate lesser/magnitude actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Gap between expectation and result opens, the audience realizes this is a point of no return; minimal efforts won't work, and all actions of lesser magnitude must be eliminated from the story thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each time the protagonist escalates and the world reacts, another point of no return closes off smaller options; the narrative must continue escalating toward an action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anti-progressive repetition; invent sufficient scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A film must not recycle actions of lesser quality in Act Two; failing to build progressions produces a 'soft belly' mid-film where audience interest wanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A feature Archplot often needs 40–60 scenes that conspire into 12–18 sequences across three+ acts; invent hundreds of ideas in research and tunnel down to the gems that will build memorable points of no return.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Law of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing moves forward in a story except through conflict. Conflict is the temporal engine of story, analogous to sound in music, that captures attention and makes time vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict must be meaningful and honestly expressed. Avoid two failures: a glut of meaningless/absurdly violent conflict (phony, overwrought mayhem) and a vacancy of meaningful conflict (tedious portraits avoiding struggle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict must be honest and appropriately leveled (quantity constant)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the quality of conflict changes as it shifts from level to level, the quantity of conflict in life is constant. Removing conflict from one level amplifies it on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If external desires are satisfied, inner conflict (boredom, lack of desire) grows. Writers should respect scarcity/limitedness as a source of honest conflict and resist replacing authentic struggle with contrived spectacle or avoiding conflict entirely.
